in.other_title: Debate on TruthfulQA: judge (Guard) performance scales with general intelligence while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant
in.rationale: Kenton et al. report stronger debaters (higher Elo) yield higher judge accuracy on extractive tasks with a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge, but are less differentiated on closed tasks. Engels et al. report that on TruthfulQA debater (Houdini) performance stays constant while the judge's (Guard's) performance scales with general intelligence rating, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA and mostly flat performance for both roles on BoolQ; they relate performance to general intelligence rating, whereas Kenton et al. relate judge accuracy to debaters' aggregate Elo.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: how debater and judge capability shape debate outcomes for LLMs

open_obligations: Check that Kenton et al.'s Elo-vs-accuracy result is positive for the extractive QA (reading comprehension) tasks specifically

Check whether this result also bears on Kenton et al.'s open question about training debaters (OPEN-TRAINING record)
in.other_title: Positive judge-accuracy trend from inference-time debate optimization (Khan et al.; Kenton et al.) persists with debate training
in.rationale: This is an explicit claim that the authors' training result agrees with Kenton et al.'s inference-time result. Kenton et al.'s passage shows that on extractive tasks stronger debaters have higher aggregate Elo and lead to higher judge accuracy, while on closed tasks there is less differentiation between debaters.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Debater strength vs judge accuracy; agreement is limited to the extractive tasks where Kenton et al. report the trend

open_obligations: Check whether the citing claim refers to Kenton et al.'s debater-Elo result or to a Kenton et al. finding about stronger judge models that the cited passage does not show and that has no dedicated record

in.other_title: Debate judge (Guard) scaling on TruthfulQA is consistent with Kenton et al.'s finding that better models may improve judge accuracy
in.rationale: The authors explicitly state consistency with prior work including Kenton et al., which they describe as finding that judge accuracy may improve with using better models. Kenton et al. report that, with Pro 1.5 as judge, stronger debaters have higher aggregate Elo and lead to higher judge accuracy on extractive tasks, with less differentiation on closed tasks. The citing work finds that the Guard's (judge's) performance scales with general intelligence rating while Houdini performance stays constant, so it varies the judge where Kenton et al. vary the debaters.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: Whether debate judge accuracy improves with stronger models; Engels et al. vary the judge (Guard), whose performance scales with general intelligence rating on TruthfulQA, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA and mostly flat performance on BoolQ, while Kenton et al. vary the debaters with Pro 1.5 as judge and find higher judge accuracy on extractive tasks but less differentiation on closed tasks; per Engels et al., prior work including Kenton et al. tests only a few models, and the Guard's 'performance' against general intelligence rating is not shown to be the same measure as Kenton et al.'s judge accuracy against debater aggregate Elo

open_obligations: Check whether the debater Elo ranges in the two tournaments are comparable.

Check whether Kenton et al.'s QuALITY-only subset shows the Khan et al. trend.
out.other_title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
out.rationale: Khan et al. report that the Elo advantage of being assigned the correct answer increases for models with higher aggregate Elo in QuALITY debates, and that this holds across different judges. Kenton et al. find a positive correct-answer Elo advantage for every debater but not as clear a trend of it growing with aggregate Elo (slightly easier for honest debaters on extractive tasks, less clear on closed tasks), with a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge across extractive and closed tasks.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether the advantage of arguing the correct answer grows with debater strength, in LLM debate cross-play tournaments

text: The paper reports that every debater has a positive Elo advantage when assigned the correct answer, but unlike Khan et al. (2024) there is no clear trend of this advantage growing with aggregate Elo. With Gemini Pro 1.5 judging, stronger debaters have higher Elo and yield higher judge accuracy on extractive tasks, while on closed tasks debaters are less differentiated in both Elo and judge accuracy.
title: Debater strength (Elo) vs judge accuracy and correct-answer advantage in debate
